turns.q: What hostname do I use to log in to Lawrencium, and what credentials?
turns.answer:
To log in to Lawrencium, use the following hostname:
`lrc-login.lbl.gov` [3, 5, 6]

For credentials, you must use Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) via Google Authenticator to generate a one-time password (OTP). When prompted for a password, enter your PIN+OTP without any spaces (for example, if your PIN is `0123` and OTP is `456789`, enter `0123456789`) [5].

You can log in using an SSH client or terminal with the command:
```bash
ssh your-username@lrc-login.lbl.gov
```
[5]

turns.q: How do I get a Lawrencium user account?
turns.answer:
To get a Lawrencium user account, you must join a project; you do not request a user account separately [Using the MyLRC Portal](https://scienceit-docs.lbl.gov/hpc/accounts/mylrc/#get-a-lawrencium-user-account).

**Process:**
1. **MyLRC Portal:** Use the [MyLRC portal](https://mylrc.lbl.gov/) to submit a user account creation request. This request can be placed by either the user or the Principal Investigator (PI) [FAQs](https://scienceit-docs.lbl.gov/hpc/faqs/).
2. **Registration & Agreement:** 
    * Sign in to [https://mylrc.lbl.gov](https://mylrc.lbl.gov/) via CILogon using your institution's identity [Using the MyLRC Portal](https://scienceit-docs.lbl.gov/hpc/accounts/mylrc/#create-your-mylrc-account).
    * Follow the registration instructions [Using the MyLRC Portal](https://scienceit-docs.lbl.gov/hpc/accounts/mylrc/#create-your-mylrc-account).
    * Sign the cluster User Access Agreement on the **Welcome** page [Using the MyLRC Portal](https://scienceit-docs.lbl.gov/hpc/accounts/mylrc/#create-your-mylrc-account).
3. **Approval:** A PI or project manager must approve the request [Using the MyLRC Portal](https://scienceit-docs.lbl.gov/hpc/accounts/mylrc/#get-a-lawrencium-user-account).
4. **Activation:** Once approved and processed, you will receive a confirmation email with instructions for logging in [Using the MyLRC Portal](https://scienceit-docs.lbl.gov/hpc/accounts/mylrc/#get-a-lawrencium-user-account).

Completion of the request through the portal is also required to obtain your account and your one-time password token generator [User Accounts](https://scienceit-docs.lbl.gov/hpc/accounts/user-accounts/#how-to-get-a-user-account-on-lawrencium-how-to-add-additional-users-to-your-project).

turns.q: Can I run jobs on the login node?
turns.answer: No, you should not run any applications, tasks, or submit jobs on the login nodes as they are shared with other cluster users [4, 7]. Instead, you should use the SLURM job scheduler to request a compute node through either an interactive or batch session [4, 7].

turns.answer: For the Lawrencium supercluster and the ETNA cluster, you should use the dedicated data transfer server (DTN) at `lrc-xfer.lbl.gov` [1, 4, 5].

turns.q: Where can I put temp files for fast I/O during a job?
turns.answer:
For fast I/O during a job, you can use the following locations on a compute node:

*   **/tmp**: This directory is mapped to the compute node's local storage and may provide faster I/O than scratch. Note that `/tmp` is only available while your job is running; any data needed later must be copied to another location (such as your HOME or SCRATCH directory) before the job terminates.
*   **/dev/shm**: This provides a small, fast temporary filesystem space that resides in RAM (memory).

[FAQs](https://scienceit-docs.lbl.gov/hpc/faqs/)

turns.q: Why am I being charged every month when I haven't run any jobs?
turns.answer:
Every Lawrencium user account is charged a **$25/month account fee (LRCACT)** for account maintenance and home directory backups [3](https://scienceit-docs.lbl.gov/hpc/accounts/charges/), [5](https://scienceit-docs.lbl.gov/hpc/accounts/project-accounts/#allocations).

This fee is separate from compute charges and is applied every month as long as the user account and its home directory exist, regardless of:
* Whether any jobs were run that month [2](https://scienceit-docs.lbl.gov/hpc/faqs/), [3](https://scienceit-docs.lbl.gov/hpc/accounts/charges/).
* The type of project the user belongs to (PCA, Condo, or Recharge) [3](https://scienceit-docs.lbl.gov/hpc/accounts/charges/), [6](https://scienceit-docs.lbl.gov/hpc/getting-started/#project-accounts).
* Whether the user still belongs to a project or if the account is blocked from logging in [3](https://scienceit-docs.lbl.gov/hpc/accounts/charges/).

User accounts are not closed automatically when a user stops running jobs or leaves the Lab [4](https://scienceit-docs.lbl.gov/hpc/accounts/charges/#account-fee-lrcact). The only way to stop this charge is to close the user account [3](https://scienceit-docs.lbl.gov/hpc/accounts/charges/).

turns.q: How do I get an AWS account through the lab?
turns.answer:
To get an AWS account through LBNL, you must work with the Science IT cloud team as users cannot self-register using their LBL identity [Requesting an AWS Account at LBNL](https://scienceit-docs.lbl.gov/cloud/aws/).

**Prerequisites**
* You must be an LBNL staff member to obtain an account [Requesting an AWS Account at LBNL](https://scienceit-docs.lbl.gov/cloud/aws/). 
* Interns and external collaborators are not eligible for their own accounts but can be provided access via IAM logins by an LBNL staff member who serves as the point of contact [Requesting an AWS Account at LBNL](https://scienceit-docs.lbl.gov/cloud/aws/).

**Request Process**
1. **Email the Science IT Cloud Team:** Send a request to `scienceit@lbl.gov` [Requesting an AWS Account at LBNL › Requesting an AWS Account](https://scienceit-docs.lbl.gov/cloud/aws/#requesting-an-aws-account).
2. **Provide Information:** In your email, include:
   * A Project ID (PID) for recharges [Requesting an AWS Account at LBNL › Requesting an AWS Account](https://scienceit-docs.lbl.gov/cloud/aws/#requesting-an-aws-account).
   * Whether you or someone else will be the account "owner" and contact [Requesting an AWS Account at LBNL › Requesting an AWS Account](https://scienceit-docs.lbl.gov/cloud/aws/#requesting-an-aws-account).
3. **Account Configuration:** The Science IT cloud team will schedule a meeting with the account owner to create and configure the account [Requesting an AWS Account at LBNL › Requesting an AWS Account](https://scienceit-docs.lbl.gov/cloud/aws/#requesting-an-aws-account).
4. **Enable MFA:** Multi-factor authentication (MFA) is mandatory for all users, including the root user and all IAM users, and must be enabled before the account can be used [Requesting an AWS Account at LBNL › Requesting an AWS Account](https://scienceit-docs.lbl.gov/cloud/aws/#requesting-an-aws-account), [Requesting an AWS Account at LBNL › Important Notes](https://scienceit-docs.lbl.gov/cloud/aws/#important-notes).

**Costs**
There are no fees for having an account; you only pay for the services and resources used. Charges are applied monthly via recharge using the Project ID, and an 11% overhead fee (procurement pass-through burden) is charged [Cloud Services](https://scienceit-docs.lbl.gov/cloud/).

turns.q: Write a batch script for a single-GPU PyTorch job.
turns.answer:
Assuming you are using the `es1` partition with an NVIDIA A40 GPU, here is an example batch script for a single-GPU PyTorch job:

```bash
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=test
#SBATCH --account=account_name
#SBATCH --partition=es1
#SBATCH --qos=es_normal
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=16
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:A40:1
#SBATCH --time=1:00:00

module load ml/pytorch
python train.py
```

[Einsteinium GPU Cluster › es1 Partition › How to specify desired GPU card(s)](https://scienceit-docs.lbl.gov/hpc/systems/einsteinium/#how-to-specify-desired-gpu-cards_2)

turns.q: How do I add my own conda environment as a Jupyter kernel in OnDemand?
turns.answer:
To add a conda environment as a Jupyter kernel in Open OnDemand, follow these steps (replace `$ENV_NAME` with the name you want for your environment):

```bash
module load miniforge3
conda create --name=$ENV_NAME ipykernel
conda activate $ENV_NAME
python -m ipykernel install --user --name $ENV_NAME
```

Once these steps are complete, you can select the environment name from the kernel list within your Jupyter environment on Open OnDemand [Adding Packages and Kernels › Adding New Kernels › Using a conda environment](https://scienceit-docs.lbl.gov/hpc/openondemand/packages-kernels/#using-a-conda-environment).

turns.q: How do I run an LLM with Ollama or vLLM on Lawrencium?
turns.answer:
### vLLM
vLLM is provided as a module and should be run only on compute nodes, preferably using newer GPUs on the `es2` partition [vLLM on Lawrencium](https://scienceit-docs.lbl.gov/hpc/software/llms/vllm/).

**Interactive Allocation:**
1. Request an allocation (example):
   ```bash
   srun -p es2 -q es2_normal --gres=gpu:H100:1 -A account_name -N 1 -t 1:00:00 --cpus-per-task=14 --pty bash
   ```
2. Load the module:
   ```bash
   module load ai/vllm/0.19.0
   ```
3. Set the model cache directory for read-only access to the central repository:
   ```bash
   export HF_HOME=/global/scratch/collections/vllm
   ```
4. Serve a model (example):
   ```bash
   vllm serve openai/gpt-oss-20b --gpu-memory-utilization=0.85
   ```

**Interacting with vLLM:**
* **Port:** vLLM serves on port `8000` by default (use `--port` to change it).
* **Accessing a running job:** To get a shell inside your job allocation, use:
  ```bash
  srun --jobid=JOBID --overlap --pty bash
  ```
* **Listing models:** 
  ```bash
  curl http://localhost:8000/v1/models
  ```
[vLLM on Lawrencium](https://scienceit-docs.lbl.gov/hpc/software/llms/vllm/)

---

### Ollama
Ollama should only be run on compute nodes. While CPU partitions can be used for small models, GPU partitions (`es0` or `es1`) provide better performance [Ollama on Lawrencium](https://scienceit-docs.lbl.gov/hpc/software/llms/ollama/).

**Option 1: Interactive Allocation**
1. Request an allocation (example):
   ```bash
   srun -p es0 -A account_name -q es_normal -N 1 -t 1:00:00 --gres=gpu:2 --cpus-per-task=2 --pty bash
   ```
2. Load a module (e.g., `ai/ollama/0.20.7`, `ai/ollama/0.12.6`, or `ai/ollama/0.6.8`) [Ollama on Lawrencium](https://scienceit-docs.lbl.gov/hpc/software/llms/ollama/).
3. Launch the server in the background:
   ```bash
   ollama serve > /dev/null 2>&1 &
   ```
4. List available models:
   ```bash
   ollama list
   ```
5. Run a model for a terminal chat interface:
   ```bash
   ollama run <model_name>
   ```

**Option 2: Open OnDemand**
You can use the **Ollama - JupyterAI & VS Code** app on LRC Open OnDemand. It is recommended to choose the `es0` or `es1` partition [Using Ollama with Jupyter and VS Code](https://scienceit-docs.lbl.gov/hpc/openondemand/ollama-jupyter-vscode/).

**Additional Ollama Tips:**
* **Saving responses:** `ollama run <model_name> "Your prompt" > response.txt`
* **Batch scripts:** Add a `sleep 10` command after `ollama serve` to allow the server time to start [Ollama on Lawrencium](https://scienceit-docs.lbl.gov/hpc/software/llms/ollama/).

turns.q: How do I build and run an Apptainer container on the cluster?
turns.answer:
### Building an Apptainer Container
You can build an image from a definition file using the following command:
```
apptainer build [name].sif [definition file]
```
For example: `apptainer build pytorch.sif pytorch.def`. Apptainer's fakeroot mode is used automatically for unprivileged users, so `--fakeroot` is not required [1].

Alternatively, you can obtain a container by pulling one from an OCI registry (like Docker Hub) and converting it to a `.sif` file:
```
apptainer pull [name].sif docker://[image path]
```
Example: `apptainer pull pytorch.sif docker://nvcr.io/nvidia/pytorch:26.07-py3` [2].

**Important Considerations:**
* **Architecture:** Lawrencium compute nodes are `x86_64` (`amd64`). Images built for `arm64` will not run on them [3]. If building a Docker image on an Apple Silicon Mac to push to a registry, use the `--platform linux/amd64` flag [3].
* **Storage:** When pulling images, you can use your `scratch` directory by setting the following environment variables [4]:
  ```
  export APPTAINER_CACHEDIR=$SCRATCH
  export APPTAINER_TMPDIR=$SCRATCH
  ```

### Running an Apptainer Container
There are three primary ways to run a container [1]:

| Command | Purpose | Syntax |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `apptainer exec` | Runs a single command inside the container, then exits | `apptainer exec [container] [command]` |
| `apptainer shell` | Opens an interactive shell inside the container | `apptainer shell [container]` |
| `apptainer run` | Runs the container's default runscript (`%runscript`), if available | `apptainer run [container]` |

**Examples:**
* `apptainer exec pytorch.sif python -c "import torch; print(torch.__version__)"` [1]
* `apptainer shell pytorch.sif` [1]
* `apptainer run pytorch.sif my_script.py` [1]

For GPU support, use the `--nv` flag, and use `--bind` to mount host directories to the container [8]:
```
apptainer exec --nv --bind /path/to/host_dir:/path/to/container_dir [container].sif [command]
```

turns.q: How do I move data from Google Drive or an S3 bucket to Lawrencium?
turns.answer:
To move data from Google Drive or an S3 bucket to Lawrencium, you can use Globus, which is a data transfer and storage service designed to move large amounts of data between resources [Globus](https://scienceit-docs.lbl.gov/data/globus/).

### From Google Drive
1. Search for [LBNL Gdrive Access](https://globus.lbl.gov/file-manager/collections/37286b85-fa2d-41bd-8110-f3ed7df32d62/) and click on the endpoint [Globus for Google Drive](https://scienceit-docs.lbl.gov/data/globus-google-drive/).
2. Click the **Collections** tab, authenticate if prompted, and select **Add a Guest Collection** [Globus for Google Drive](https://scienceit-docs.lbl.gov/data/globus-google-drive/).
3. Enter the drive path you wish to view, select a display name, and click **Create Collection** [Globus for Google Drive](https://scienceit-docs.lbl.gov/data/globus-google-drive/).
4. Return to the **Endpoint** tab, search for your collection by its display name, and open it in the File Manager to perform the transfer [Globus for Google Drive](https://scienceit-docs.lbl.gov/data/globus-google-drive/).

### From an S3 Bucket
1. Log in to [https://globus.lbl.gov](https://globus.lbl.gov/) and select **Endpoints** from the left navigation [Using the Globus AWS S3 Connector › Select Globus S3 Endpoint](https://scienceit-docs.lbl.gov/data/globus-aws-s3-connector/#select-globus-s3-endpoint).
2. Search for and click on the **LBNL AWS S3 Collection** [Using the Globus AWS S3 Connector › Select Globus S3 Endpoint](https://scienceit-docs.lbl.gov/data/globus-aws-s3-connector/#select-globus-s3-endpoint).
3. In the **Credentials** tab, register your AWS IAM access key ID and secret key [Using the Globus AWS S3 Connector › Select Globus S3 Endpoint](https://scienceit-docs.lbl.gov/data/globus-aws-s3-connector/#select-globus-s3-endpoint).
4. Go to the **Overview** tab and click **Open in File Manager** to access your S3 buckets and transfer the data [Using the Globus AWS S3 Connector › Select Globus S3 Endpoint](https://scienceit-docs.lbl.gov/data/globus-aws-s3-connector/#select-globus-s3-endpoint).

For transfers to Lawrencium, the cluster's dedicated Data Transfer Node is `lrc-xfer.lbl.gov` [Getting Started › Data Movement and Storage](https://scienceit-docs.lbl.gov/hpc/getting-started/#data-movement-and-storage).

turns.q: I'm a new student. Walk me through everything from getting an account to running my first GPU job.
turns.answer:
### 1. Getting an Account
To obtain an account, you must complete user account requests at the [myLRC portal](https://mylrc.lbl.gov/). Accounts are added upon approval of the project PI. Through this portal, you will receive your account and a one-time password token generator [Source 4].

### 2. Logging In
You can login to the cluster using the server name `lrc-login.lbl.gov` with your username and PIN+OTP combination [Source 2]. 

**Important:** You land on a login node, which is shared with other users. You should use these nodes to edit scripts or compile programs, but you must **not** run applications or tasks on them [Source 2, Source 3].

### 3. Running Your First GPU Job
You can run GPU jobs either via a batch script or an interactive session through Open OnDemand.

#### Option A: Batch Slurm Script
To run a job non-interactively, create a Slurm script and submit it using `sbatch` [Source 5]. For the `es1` partition, use the following parameters [Source 8]:
- **Partition:** `es1`
- **QoS:** `es_normal`
- **GPU Request:** Use `--gres=gpu:[type]:[count]` (e.g., `--gres=gpu:A40:1`).
- **CPU Ratio:** You must maintain a specific CPU-to-GPU ratio. For example, requesting one A40 GPU requires `--cpus-per-task=16` [Source 8].

**Example script for one NVIDIA A40 GPU:**
```bash
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=test
#SBATCH --account=account_name
#SBATCH --partition=es1
#SBATCH --qos=es_normal
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=16
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:A40:1
#SBATCH --time=1:00:00

module load ml/pytorch
python train.py
```

#### Option B: Interactive Session (Open OnDemand)
You can launch interactive apps like Jupyter notebooks via [https://lrc-ondemand.lbl.gov](https://lrc-ondemand.lbl.gov) using CILogon [Source 3]. To launch a Jupyter Server on one A40 GPU card [Source 1]:
1. **SLURM Partition:** `es1`
2. **Name of SLURM Quality of Service (QoS):** `es_normal`
3. **Number of nodes:** `1`
4. **GPU Type:** `es1: NVidia A40 (40 GB) 1-4x`
5. **Number of GPU cards to use:** `1`
6. Enter your **SLURM Project/Account Name**, **Wall Clock Time**, and **Name of the job**.
7. Click **Launch**, and once ready, click **Connect to Jupyter**.

If you encounter issues, contact the HPC help desk at scienceithelp@lbl.gov [Source 4].

turns.q: My job reads a huge dataset and is I/O bound. What should I change?
turns.answer:
For jobs with high I/O requirements, you should make the following changes:

*   **Use the SCRATCH filesystem**: Use `SCRATCH` when your job needs to read or write large amounts of data, as it is designed specifically for this purpose [1, 3].
*   **Avoid Enterprise Storage**: Do not run large I/O dependent jobs on HOME, GROUP, or GROUP-SW directories, as this can degrade performance for other users and may result in your job being killed without notification [1].
*   **Utilize Local Storage for Caching**: For faster I/O than scratch, use the `/tmp` directory on the compute node to cache datasets and intermediate files during the job. Note that data in `/tmp` must be copied to your HOME or SCRATCH directory before the job terminates [7].
*   **Use RAM for Small Files**: Consider using `/dev/shm` for small, fast temporary filesystem space that resides in RAM [7].

turns.q: I need to run 500 small independent tasks. What's the best approach?
turns.answer:
For running many small independent tasks, the best approach is to use **GNU Parallel** within a SLURM job. This allows you to automate and parallelize tasks across multiple cores or nodes.

Based on the documentation, the implementation involves three components:

1.  **A Task List**: A file (e.g., `task.lst`) where each line contains the parameters for one task [GNU Parallel › Basic Usage › Extended example](https://scienceit-docs.lbl.gov/hpc/running/gnu-parallel/#extended-example).
2.  **A Serial Bash Script**: A script that performs a single task using the parameters provided by GNU Parallel [GNU Parallel › Basic Usage › Extended example](https://scienceit-docs.lbl.gov/hpc/running/gnu-parallel/#extended-example).
3.  **A SLURM Submission Script**: A script that requests resources and launches GNU Parallel.

### Example Implementation
You can use the following structure for your SLURM script:

```bash
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=job-name
#SBATCH --account=account_name
#SBATCH --partition=partition_name
#SBATCH --qos=qos_name
#SBATCH --nodes=2
#SBATCH --time=2:00:00

module load parallel
export WDIR=/your/desired/path
cd $WDIR
export JOBS_PER_NODE=$SLURM_CPUS_ON_NODE

# Create a hostfile from the SLURM node list
echo $SLURM_JOB_NODELIST | sed s/\,/\\n/g > hostfile

# Launch tasks in parallel
parallel --jobs $JOBS_PER_NODE --slf hostfile --wd $WDIR --joblog task.log --resume --progress \
--colsep ' ' -a task.lst sh run-task.sh {} output/{/.}.out
```
[GNU Parallel › Basic Usage › Extended example](https://scienceit-docs.lbl.gov/hpc/running/gnu-parallel/#extended-example)

### Useful GNU Parallel Flags
*   `-a`: Specify the task list as input [GNU Parallel › Basic Usage › Extended example](https://scienceit-docs.lbl.gov/hpc/running/gnu-parallel/#extended-example).
*   `--jobs`: Define the number of tasks per node [GNU Parallel › Basic Usage › Extended example](https://scienceit-docs.lbl.gov/hpc/running/gnu-parallel/#extended-example).
*   `--slf`: Provide the compute node list [GNU Parallel › Basic Usage › Extended example](https://scienceit-docs.lbl.gov/hpc/running/gnu-parallel/#extended-example).
*   `--joblog` and `--resume`: Use these together to keep track of completed tasks and allow the job to resume from where it left off [GNU Parallel › Basic Usage › Extended example](https://scienceit-docs.lbl.gov/hpc/running/gnu-parallel/#extended-example).
*   `--progress`: Display the progress of the jobs [GNU Parallel › Basic Usage › Extended example](https://scienceit-docs.lbl.gov/hpc/running/gnu-parallel/#extended-example).
*   `--wd`: Set the landing working directory on compute nodes (defaults to `$HOME`) [GNU Parallel › Basic Usage › Extended example](https://scienceit-docs.lbl.gov/hpc/running/gnu-parallel/#extended-example).

turns.q: How do I get GPUs?
turns.answer:
You can get GPUs on Lawrencium through Slurm job submissions or via Open Ondemand.

### Via Slurm
You can request GPUs by specifying the partition and the generic resource (`--gres`). The general format is `--gres=gpu:[type]:count` [Example Scripts › GPU Job](https://scienceit-docs.lbl.gov/hpc/running/script-examples/#gpu-job).

**Available Partitions and GPUs:**
*   **`es2`**: NVIDIA H100 (up to 8 GPUs) and H200 (up to 8 GPUs) [Example Scripts › GPU Job](https://scienceit-docs.lbl.gov/hpc/running/script-examples/#gpu-job), [Einsteinium GPU Cluster › es2 Partition](https://scienceit-docs.lbl.gov/hpc/systems/einsteinium/#es2-partition).
*   **`es1`**: V100 (up to 2 GPUs), A40 (up to 4 GPUs), and GTX 2080TI [Example Scripts › GPU Job](https://scienceit-docs.lbl.gov/hpc/running/script-examples/#gpu-job).
*   **`es0`**: NVIDIA 2080TI [Einsteinium GPU Cluster › es0 Partition](https://scienceit-docs.lbl.gov/hpc/systems/einsteinium/#es0-partition).

**Important Requirements:**
You must request sufficient CPUs for every GPU used, or the scheduler will reject the job [Example Scripts › GPU Job](https://scienceit-docs.lbl.gov/hpc/running/script-examples/#gpu-job). The required CPU:GPU ratios are:
*   **H100/H200**: 1:14 [Example Scripts › GPU Job › CPU Core to GPU Ratio](https://scienceit-docs.lbl.gov/hpc/running/script-examples/#cpu-core-to-gpu-ratio)
*   **A40/A100/GRTX8000**: 1:16 [Example Scripts › GPU Job › CPU Core to GPU Ratio](https://scienceit-docs.lbl.gov/hpc/running/script-examples/#cpu-core-to-gpu-ratio)
*   **V100**: 1:4 [Example Scripts › GPU Job › CPU Core to GPU Ratio](https://scienceit-docs.lbl.gov/hpc/running/script-examples/#cpu-core-to-gpu-ratio)

**Example Slurm Requests:**
*   One A40 GPU on `es1`:
    ```bash
    --partition=es1 --cpus-per-task=16 --gres=gpu:A40:1 --ntasks=1
    ```
*   Three H100 GPUs on `es2`:
    ```bash
    --partition=es2 --cpus-per-task=14 --gres=gpu:H100:3 --ntasks=3
    ```
*   One V100 GPU on `es1`:
    ```bash
    --partition=es1 --cpus-per-task=4 --gres=gpu:V100:1 --ntasks=1
    ```
(Source: [Example Scripts › GPU Job › CPU Core to GPU Ratio](https://scienceit-docs.lbl.gov/hpc/running/script-examples/#cpu-core-to-gpu-ratio))

### Via Open Ondemand
For running LLMs, you can use the **Ollama - JupyterAI & VS Code** app on LRC Open Ondemand. In the app's requirements form, select your preferred partition (GPU nodes `es0` or `es1` are recommended), GPU type, and number of GPUs [Using Ollama with Jupyter and VS Code](https://scienceit-docs.lbl.gov/hpc/openondemand/ollama-jupyter-vscode/).

turns.q: how 2 check my jobs
turns.answer:
Depending on whether your jobs are currently running or have already finished, you can use the following methods:

### Running Jobs
**Command Line:**
* To list your current jobs and find your SLURM job ID, run:
  ```bash
  squeue -u $USER
  ```
  [[Monitor Jobs](https://scienceit-docs.lbl.gov/hpc/running/monitor-jobs/#monitoring-the-status-of-running-batch-jobs), [Slurm Overview](https://scienceit-docs.lbl.gov/hpc/running/slurm-overview/)]
* To check the status of the node your job is running on, use `wwall`:
    * For a snapshot: `wwall -j $your_job_id`
    * For a text-based user interface (TUI): `wwall -j $your_job_id -t` (press "q" to quit)
  [[Monitor Jobs](https://scienceit-docs.lbl.gov/hpc/running/monitor-jobs/#monitoring-the-status-of-running-batch-jobs)]
* To see a "top"-like summary for all nodes, run `wwtop` from a login node [[Monitor Jobs](https://scienceit-docs.lbl.gov/hpc/running/monitor-jobs/#monitoring-the-status-of-running-batch-jobs)].

**Portals:**
* **MyLRC Portal:** Click **Jobs** in the menu bar, use the filter to find your job, and click its job ID for details [[Using the MyLRC Portal › Check usage and jobs](https://scienceit-docs.lbl.gov/hpc/accounts/mylrc/#check-usage-and-jobs)].
* **Open OnDemand:** View all currently running jobs under `Jobs > Active Jobs` or specific interactive sessions under `My Interactive Sessions` [[Open OnDemand Overview › Service Unit Charges](https://scienceit-docs.lbl.gov/hpc/openondemand/overview/#service-unit-charges)].

### Finished Jobs
**Command Line:**
* **Logs:** Check the `slurm-.out` and `slurm-.err` files in the directory where the job was submitted [[Checking finished jobs](https://scienceit-docs.lbl.gov/hpc/running/monitor-jobs/#checking-finished-jobs)].
* **Memory Usage:** Use the `sacct` command to see the maximum memory used (MaxRSS in kilobytes):
  ```bash
  sacct -j –format=JobID,JobName,MaxRSS,Elapsed
  ```
  [[Checking finished jobs](https://scienceit-docs.lbl.gov/hpc/running/monitor-jobs/#checking-finished-jobs)]
* **Job History:** Check all jobs run within a specific time window:
  ```bash
  sacct -u –starttime=YYYY-MM-DD –endtime=YYYY-MM-DD \
  –format JobID,JobName,Partition,Account,AllocCPUS,State,ExitCode,Start,End,NodeList
  ```
  [[Checking finished jobs](https://scienceit-docs.lbl.gov/hpc/running/monitor-jobs/#checking-finished-jobs)]

turns.q: sbatch says invalid account/partition combination, help
turns.answer:
To resolve an invalid account/partition combination error, you must ensure that the account, partition, and QoS (Quality of Service) are paired correctly in your job submission script.

You can check the combinations available to you by running the following command:

```bash
sacctmgr show association -p user=$USER
```

The output of this command will show each valid combination of account, partition, and QoS that you can use when submitting a batch job [Slurm Overview › Slurm Association](https://scienceit-docs.lbl.gov/hpc/running/slurm-overview/#slurm-association).

turns.q: lawrencium vs einsteinium?
turns.answer:
Based on the provided documentation, the primary difference is their hardware focus:

*   **Lawrencium** is a CPU cluster [Hardware Configuration](https://scienceit-docs.lbl.gov/hpc/#hardware-configuration).
*   **Einsteinium** is an institutional GPU cluster designed for researchers performing deep learning and machine learning [Einsteinium GPU Cluster](https://scienceit-docs.lbl.gov/hpc/systems/einsteinium/).

**Einsteinium Details:**
*   **Purpose:** Meeting computational demand for AI/ML workflows [Einsteinium GPU Cluster](https://scienceit-docs.lbl.gov/hpc/systems/einsteinium/).
*   **Example Partition (`es3`):** Consists of 12 nodes with AMD EPYC 9754 processors and 4x NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPUs (96 GB memory each) per node [Einsteinium GPU Cluster](https://scienceit-docs.lbl.gov/hpc/systems/einsteinium/). Other mentioned partitions include `es2`, `es1`, and `es0` [AlphaFold 3 on Lawrencium › Running](https://scienceit-docs.lbl.gov/hpc/software/ml/alphafold3/#running), [Using Claude Science with Lawrencium › Host notes for Lawrencium](https://scienceit-docs.lbl.gov/hpc/ai-tools/claude-science/#host-notes-for-lawrencium).

turns.q: Give me a command for a 1-hour interactive session on lr4.
turns.answer:
You can use the following command for a 1-hour interactive session on lr4:

```bash
srun -p lr4 -A account_name -q lr_normal -N 1 -t 1:00:00 --pty bash
```
*(Note: Replace `account_name` with your actual account name.)*

[Slurm Overview](https://scienceit-docs.lbl.gov/hpc/running/slurm-overview/)

turns.q: now make it a GPU node
turns.answer:
For a 1-hour interactive session on a GPU node (using the `es2` partition as an example), you can use the following command:

```bash
srun -p es2 -q es2_normal --gres=gpu:H100:1 -A account_name -N 1 -t 1:00:00 --cpus-per-task=14 --pty bash
```

*(Note: Replace `account_name` with your actual account name.)*

[vLLM on Lawrencium](https://scienceit-docs.lbl.gov/hpc/software/llms/vllm/)

turns.q: make it 2 nodes for 6 hours
turns.answer:

```bash
srun -p es0 -A account_name -q es_normal -N 2 -t 6:00:00 --gres=gpu:2 --cpus-per-task=2 --pty bash
```

*(Note: Replace `account_name` with your actual account name.)*

[Ollama on Lawrencium](https://scienceit-docs.lbl.gov/hpc/software/llms/ollama/)
